## TL;DR

Task #1211 was a read-only QA pass: compare the runner setup recipes in
`justfile` and the runner health screens with how the bee, thinkpad and mini
runners are actually provisioned, and fix stale docs or UI wording — without
SSHing to any runner. The comparison found one real gap: nothing in the docs or
the Runners view explained the account boundary, i.e. that `user@host` is the
remote SSH login while the RepoOS server process (especially a systemd service)
is a separate identity that needs its own SSH key and host-key trust. I fixed
that in the setup docs, the end-user check docs and a new note on the Remote
runners panel, with regression tests tying the wording to the actual recipes.
One violation of the task's no-SSH constraint did occur and cannot be undone:
the first required check unexpectedly started Tailscale remote validation and
probed `nick@thinkpad` once before I interrupted it. Its output was discarded,
it changed nothing on any runner (the probe only runs `true` remotely and pipes
to `/dev/null`), and no SSH was used afterwards. The QA record states this
plainly.

## Work and rationale

I started by reading the three setup recipes in `justfile` (`setup-bee`,
`setup-thinkpad`, `setup-mini`, plus the `native` variants and their shared
`_setup-runner` / `_setup-runner-native` helpers) and treating them as ground
truth for how the machines are provisioned, since the task says the recipes
describe how the runners are actually run. Then I compared that against
`docs/remote-validation.md`, the runner section of `user-docs/check.md`, and
the Checks → Remote runners panel plus the health DTO it renders.

The decisive finding was account-specificity. The Docker recipes stage the
build in the SSH login's home directory, install `/opt/repoos/validate.sh` with
`sudo`, and use Docker as that SSH account (the Arch recipe adds it to the
`docker` group, warning that a new login may be needed). The native recipes
copy `validate-macos.sh` to the SSH user's `~/.local/bin/repoos-validate`
without sudo. Meanwhile the health display identifies a host as `user@host` and
runs its probes with the configured SSH identity — but nothing said that the
RepoOS server itself runs under a *different* local account, and that if that
server is a systemd service it must independently be able to authenticate to
the configured SSH host and trust its host key. A successful interactive `just
setup-...` run tells you nothing about the service account's access, which is
exactly the confusion the task's "different user than the ssh login" case
anticipates.

I fixed this in three places, keeping each audience-appropriate. The setup
material in `docs/remote-validation.md` gained the account boundary, the
recipe-specific staging destinations and permissions, and the native recipe's
non-interactive login-shell PATH behavior. `user-docs/check.md` gained a short
end-user paragraph explaining how to read the `user@host` field and why a
service-only authentication failure has a clear cause. The Remote runners panel
got a compact note (`runner-identity-note`) repeating the same three facts in
UI language: `user@host` is the SSH login, a systemd server account needs its
own credentials and trust, and ready status reflects checks as the configured
SSH user.

Two tests pin the new claims. A docs test asserts the new explanations
alongside the actual recipe markers from `justfile`, so the prose cannot drift
from the scripts it describes. A component test asserts the panel's note
wording. I also committed the QA record `docs/qa/2026-11-runner-docs.md` with
the method, findings, changes and evidence limits, including the SSH incident
described plainly.

## Approaches tried

I deliberately avoided live verification of the runners; the task forbids SSH
and the QA method is comparison of checked-in scripts and source. To confirm
the mistaken probe could not have modified a runner, I read the probe's
implementation instead of testing it remotely: it runs `true` on the remote
host and sends its payload to `cat > /dev/null`, so it never creates or alters
a remote file. After the incident, all verification ran in local-tests mode so
the gate never contacted a configured runner again.

I considered rewriting the panel more deeply (for example, displaying which
local server account is checking) and rejected it: the health DTO cannot know
the service account's credentials, and inventing UI for unverifiable state
would have been worse than the honest note.

## Challenges and blockers

The main challenge is the SSH probe itself. The first required check run
unexpectedly triggered Tailscale remote validation — the gate's remote step —
which probed `nick@thinkpad` before I interrupted it. That violated the task's
explicit no-SSH constraint and nothing can undo it. The probe made no changes
to any runner, its output was discarded, and no SSH was used afterwards, but
the violation stands and is recorded in the QA note and in review findings.

The second challenge was a rendered-contrast failure in the required check: a
large number of low-contrast settings label/description pairs in the unrelated
`gen-z-dark` theme scope. None named the changed runner panel. Fixing an
unrelated theme was out of scope, so I left it untouched and recorded it
rather than masking it or touching `repoos.toml`.

Remaining evidence limits stand: this is a comparison of checked-in scripts
and source, not a live audit. Which service user is actually deployed on each
machine, whether its SSH credentials work, and current PATH/Docker permissions
remain unverified and need a human-side check in the relevant service context.

## Key learnings

- The crux of remote-runner correctness is the account boundary: the SSH login
  that setup and probes use is not the identity of the RepoOS server process,
  and a systemd service must carry its own SSH credentials and host-key trust.
- The check gate can have remote side effects under this configuration; when a
  task forbids remote interaction, run scoped verification in local-tests mode
  from the start rather than discovering the remote step by accident.
- A QA record that states a mistake plainly — what happened, that the output
  was discarded, that nothing was changed, and that the behavior did not
  recur — is more useful to reviewers than one that buries it.
- Docs that describe scripts are safest when a test asserts both the prose and
  the script markers together, so they fail together when either drifts.
